title: Customer Service Excellence and Customer Acquisition

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the customer experience (CX) imperative in insurance and describe why CX management is a strategic function — not merely an operational support function — in the context of Nigeria’s insurance trust deficit.
Construct a customer journey map for a life insurance product, identifying the principal stages, key touchpoints, moments of truth, and the most common pain points at each stage.

Design service standards for the four principal customer touchpoint categories — contact centre, digital self-service, field operations, and claims handling — with specific reference to the Nigerian operating environment.

Define Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for key insurance customer interactions, describe how SLA compliance is monitored and escalated, and explain the link between SLA performance and customer retention.

Explain the Net Promoter Score (NPS) and three other CX measurement frameworks — Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT), Customer Effort Score (CES), and First Contact Resolution (FCR) — and describe how each is applied in insurance practice.
Describe the three components of a customer retention programme — lapse management, conservation, and policy revival — explaining the operational mechanics and financial justification for each.
Explain the cross-selling and upselling opportunity map for a life insurance customer portfolio and describe the compliance obligations that govern cross-selling to existing policyholders.
Describe four customer acquisition strategies — referral programmes, affinity groups, employer portals, and digital funnels — explaining the commercial mechanics and performance metrics of each.

Define a vulnerable customer in the insurance context, describe the identification and adapted service delivery protocols required, and explain how inclusive service design reduces vulnerability risk.
Describe NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework, the NAICOM complaints redress mechanism, and the regulatory consequences for insurers that fail to meet consumer protection obligations.

blocks.h: Customer experience (CX) is every interaction a policyholder has with an insurance company — from the first advertisement they encounter, through the sales conversation, the policy issuance, the premium payment, the annual anniversary statement, and ultimately the claims experience. Each of these interactions either strengthens or weakens the policyholder’s trust in the insurer, their likelihood of maintaining the policy, and their willingness to recommend the company to family and friends.

In most consumer industries, CX management is primarily a commercial function: companies invest in service quality because satisfied customers buy more and stay longer. In Nigerian life insurance, the commercial argument for CX excellence is even stronger — but the urgency is different. Here, CX is a trust-repair function as much as a commercial one. Every policy serviced promptly, every query answered clearly, every claim paid fairly represents a counter-narrative to the industry’s dominant negative perception. An insurer that delivers consistently excellent CX is not merely retaining customers; it is actively rebuilding public trust in the institution of insurance itself.

The CX imperative is also intensified by NIIRA 2025. The Act’s consumer protection provisions create enforceable obligations around service response times, complaint handling, claims settlement, and the treatment of vulnerable customers. CX failure is no longer merely a commercial risk — it is a regulatory risk, with NAICOM’s expanded enforcement arsenal available to respond to systemic service quality failures.

This chapter addresses the full scope of the CX and customer acquisition agenda for a Nigerian life insurer: the tools to measure and understand the customer experience, the service standards required to deliver it, the retention programmes that protect the existing portfolio, the acquisition strategies that grow it, and the regulatory framework that governs both.

blocks.text: 20.2.1 What is a Customer Journey Map?

blocks.h: A customer journey map is a structured visual representation of every significant interaction a customer has with an organisation, from the first moment of awareness through to the end of the relationship. It documents: the sequence of interactions (touchpoints); what the customer is trying to do at each stage (their goal); how the customer feels at each stage (their emotional state); and where the company is currently succeeding or failing to meet the customer’s needs (moments of truth and pain points).

For life insurance, journey mapping reveals the reality of the customer’s experience as they live it — not as the insurer designs it on paper. A sales process that looks smooth from the inside (agent contacts prospect, presents product, completes application, submits to underwriting, policy is issued, premium direct debit is set up) may look very different from the customer’s perspective: the agent took three weeks to follow up; the underwriting request for medical evidence was confusing; the direct debit instruction was not processed correctly; the policy document arrived six weeks after the first premium was deducted.

blocks.h: The term ‘moment of truth’ — coined by Jan Carlzon of SAS Airlines and extensively applied in service management — refers to the specific interaction at which the customer forms a definitive impression of the organisation that either builds or destroys their trust. For life insurance, the moments of truth are fewer than in a high-frequency transaction service, but they are disproportionately important because they occur at emotionally significant junctures: when the customer is making a major financial commitment (purchase), when they need help urgently (a service failure), or when they are at their most vulnerable (a death in the family, a critical illness diagnosis).

The claim payment is universally recognised as the ultimate moment of truth in insurance. But the policy onboarding experience, the first annual statement, and the response to the customer’s first query are also critical: they set the tone for the entire in-force relationship. An insurer that handles the first three months of a new policyholder’s experience with clarity, warmth, and speed will retain that policyholder at a materially higher rate than an insurer that loses contact with the customer after the first premium is collected.

The contact centre (whether a physical call centre or a virtual team) is the primary human-to-human service channel for most Nigerian life insurers. It is the first point of contact for policyholders with queries, complaints, claims notifications, and premium payment issues. The quality of the contact centre experience is often the primary determinant of the policyholder’s overall satisfaction with their insurer.
Key design principles for a best-practice Nigerian insurance contact centre:

items.h: Omnichannel capability: The contact centre must handle queries across all channels the customer uses: inbound telephone; WhatsApp text and voice; email; and, for digital-native products, in-app chat. Customers who have to switch channels to resolve a query — ‘call us on this number’ when they have sent a WhatsApp message — experience friction that reduces satisfaction.

Policy information at first contact: Contact centre agents must have real-time access to the customer’s complete policy record — premium status, sum assured, beneficiary, outstanding loans, claims history. A customer who has to repeat their policy details, spell out their name multiple times, or be transferred three times before their query is addressed will not renew.

Empathy-first scripting: Particularly for claims-related calls and hardship-driven lapse inquiries, contact centre agents must be trained to acknowledge the customer’s emotional state before moving to procedural responses. A recently bereaved family calling to start the claims process needs empathy before documentation.

First Contact Resolution (FCR) discipline: Every query should be resolved in the first interaction wherever possible. Queries that require escalation should be tracked to resolution with a proactive callback commitment: ‘We will call you back within 48 hours.’ Failure to meet the callback commitment is a service failure.

blocks.h: Digital self-service channels — the insurer’s mobile app, customer portal, USSD interface, and WhatsApp chatbot — enable policyholders to access information and complete routine transactions without contacting a human agent. For the policyholder, self-service offers 24/7 access and instant response. For the insurer, it reduces contact centre volume and cost while increasing policyholder engagement frequency.

Core capabilities that Nigerian life insurance digital self-service should provide: premium payment confirmation and receipt; policy summary and benefit details; beneficiary information; premium payment via card, bank transfer, or mobile money; alteration requests (name change, address update, beneficiary update) with document upload; loan application (where policy loans are available); claims notification initiation; and the ability to escalate to a human agent without loss of context.

The design of self-service interfaces for a Nigerian audience must account for the diversity of the user base: screen interfaces designed for high-literacy, smartphone-proficient users will fail the significant proportion of policyholders on low-literacy, basic smartphone, or feature phone devices. A ‘mobile-first, simple-first’ design philosophy — prioritising clarity, minimal text, visual cues, and USSD fallback for critical transactions — is essential for inclusive service design.

Despite the growth of digital channels, the field operations function — the agent who visits the policyholder at home, the branch that is physically accessible — remains critical for several categories of customer interaction: complex queries that require human explanation; in-person conservation visits when a policy is at risk of lapse; and communities where digital literacy or connectivity is insufficient for self-service. The field operations model in Nigeria must be designed for the country’s geographic and infrastructure realities: traffic congestion in Lagos, poor road conditions in some rural areas, and the concentration of policyholders in locations where branches are not economically viable.

The ‘phygital’ model — a hybrid of physical field presence and digital enablement — is the most practical for many Nigerian life insurers. Agents equipped with smartphones and the insurer’s agent app can conduct policy reviews, update beneficiary details, collect premium payments, and submit alteration requests remotely, reducing the need for physical branch visits for routine servicing while maintaining the human relationship for higher-stakes interactions.

blocks.text: 20.3.4 Claims Handling as a CX Moment

blocks.h: Every aspect of claims handling is addressed in Chapter 12. From a CX management perspective, the additional dimension is that claims handling must be designed not merely to settle valid claims correctly — that is the minimum standard — but to make the claimant feel cared for, informed, and respected throughout what is often the most stressful financial and personal experience of their life.

Best-practice CX elements of claims handling: a dedicated claims relationship manager for every open claim above a defined threshold; a guaranteed maximum of 48 hours between any documentation submission and acknowledgement of receipt; a proactive status update (by phone or WhatsApp) every five business days while the claim is open; a compassionate, plain-language declination letter that explains the specific reason for non-payment and the available recourse options; and a post-claims survey to collect feedback on the claimant’s experience.

blocks.text: 20.4.1 The Purpose of SLAs in Insurance

blocks.h: A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is a commitment by the insurer to deliver a defined standard of service within a defined timeframe. SLAs convert the subjective concept of ‘good service’ into measurable, manageable, and enforceable performance targets. They are the operational expression of the insurer’s customer promise and the measurement framework against which CX performance is assessed.

Under NIIRA 2025, some service standards are no longer discretionary. The 60-day maximum claims settlement timeline (Chapter 12, s.210) is a regulatory SLA: late settlement attracts compound interest, administrative sanctions and possible compensation. A 5-business-day claims acknowledgement is recommended practice, although no statutory acknowledgement period has been confirmed. An insurer’s internal SLA framework should be set at standards more stringent than the regulatory minimum, creating a management buffer that prevents regulatory breaches.

blocks.h: SLA compliance must be monitored in real time through the insurer’s CRM and case management systems. Every open customer interaction should have a due date (the SLA deadline) visible to the handling agent and their supervisor. Interactions approaching the SLA deadline should trigger an automated alert; interactions that breach the SLA should trigger an automatic escalation to the supervisor and a notification to the quality assurance team.

Monthly SLA compliance reporting should be presented to the Customer Experience Director and the COO. Any metric consistently below target requires a root cause investigation: Is the SLA breach due to inadequate staffing? Process complexity? Technology failure? Policy information quality? Each root cause requires a different remediation. An insurer that monitors SLA compliance but does not investigate root causes will produce the same compliance report month after month without improvement.

blocks.text: 20.5 CX Measurement: NPS and Other Metrics

blocks.h: A customer loyalty metric that measures the likelihood of a customer recommending the insurer to a friend or colleague. Customers are asked: ‘On a scale of 0–10, how likely are you to recommend [insurer] to a friend or colleague?’ Respondents scoring 9–10 are Promoters; 7–8 are Passives; 0–6 are Detractors. NPS = % Promoters − % Detractors. Scores range from −100 to +100. A positive score indicates more promoters than detractors.
NPS = (% Promoters) − (% Detractors)
Example: 400 customers surveyed. 160 score 9–10 (Promoters = 40%). 80 score 0–6 (Detractors = 20%). 160 score 7–8 (Passives). NPS = 40 − 20 = +20.

Benchmarks: NPS > 0 = more promoters than detractors (acceptable). NPS > 30 = strong loyalty. NPS > 50 = excellent. NPS < 0 = more detractors than promoters (crisis level in most markets). Nigerian insurance industry average NPS is estimated in the −5 to +10 range, reflecting the sector’s trust challenges.

NPS is a leading indicator of growth: companies with high NPS grow faster because promoters actively refer new customers. For a Nigerian life insurer, building a promoter base is particularly valuable because peer recommendation is the most trusted source of insurance information in a market where advertising scepticism is high. A policyholder who received a prompt, fair claim settlement and tells their colleagues is worth more than a full-page newspaper advertisement.

CSAT measures satisfaction with a specific interaction — ‘How satisfied were you with your claims experience today?’ (scored 1–5 or 1–10). Unlike NPS, which measures relationship-level loyalty, CSAT measures transaction-level satisfaction. It is best used immediately after a specific service interaction (post-call, post-claim, post-policy issuance) to capture the customer’s reaction to that specific touchpoint.

CSAT by touchpoint enables the insurer to identify which specific interactions are generating dissatisfaction. A high post-sales CSAT but a low post-underwriting CSAT reveals that the underwriting process (medical evidence collection, turnaround time) is the friction point. A high CSAT at policy issuance but a low CSAT at first annual statement indicates a gap in the ongoing communication experience.

CES measures how easy it was for the customer to complete an interaction: ‘The insurance company made it easy for me to handle my issue.’ (Strongly agree = 7 to Strongly disagree = 1). Research consistently shows that reducing customer effort — making it easier to interact with the insurer — has a stronger impact on loyalty than delight. A policyholder who finds it effortless to pay their premium, update their address, or submit a claim will maintain their policy far longer than one who has to struggle with every routine interaction.

In the Nigerian insurance context, the highest-effort interactions are typically: obtaining a policy document after payment; getting through to a contact centre agent; and submitting a claim — particularly gathering the required documentation. CES data on these interactions provides a direct improvement roadmap: reduce the effort at these specific points and retention will improve.

FCR measures the proportion of customer queries or complaints resolved in the first interaction, without the customer needing to call back or escalate. FCR is both a service quality metric and an operational efficiency metric: every repeat contact to resolve the same issue represents a cost to the insurer and a frustration to the customer.

Target FCR rate for a Nigerian insurance contact centre: 70%+ for standard queries (premium payment confirmation, policy balance, basic alteration requests). Complex queries (claims disputes, non-disclosure investigations, policy reinstatement) are unlikely to be resolved at first contact and should not distort the FCR metric for simple queries. FCR is best tracked by query category to identify where process improvement or agent training can increase first-contact resolution rates.

blocks.text: 20.6 Customer Retention: Lapse Management, Conservation, and Revival

blocks.h: Customer retention in life insurance is not a passive function — it is an active, structured commercial discipline. A policy that lapses represents a destroyed premium stream, a wasted acquisition cost, a policyholder left without protection, and a potential claims dispute (if the lapse was not the customer’s free choice). The financial mathematics of lapse prevention are straightforward: preventing one lapse is worth far more than acquiring one new policy, because the acquisition cost on the new policy must be paid again.

Lapse management is the systematic effort to prevent policies from lapsing — to identify at-risk policies early, diagnose the cause, and intervene before the policy moves from active to lapsed. The earlier in the lapse process an intervention occurs, the higher the success rate: a policyholder who has missed one premium is far easier to retain than one who has missed three.
A best-practice lapse management programme has four components:

items.h: Early warning system: An automated alert generated on the premium due date when the premium has not been received. The alert is sent simultaneously to the policyholder (SMS or WhatsApp reminder) and to the responsible agent. This is the first-day contact principle: reach the policyholder before they have consciously decided to lapse.

Cause diagnosis: When the agent or contact centre contacts the policyholder, the conversation must identify the reason for non-payment: affordability (the premium is too high for current income); forgotten (the debit mandate was not set up or failed); dissatisfaction (the customer intends to cancel); or administrative (a bank account change or payment routing error). Each cause requires a different response.

Tailored intervention: Affordability issues: offer to reduce the sum assured or convert to a lower-premium plan; facilitate a payment plan for arrears; explain the paid-up conversion option. Forgotten payment: resend the debit instruction; set up WhatsApp payment reminder. Dissatisfaction: route to a senior agent or customer experience manager for a conservation conversation.

Grace period management: Most Nigerian life policies provide a 30-day grace period after the premium due date during which the policy remains in force. Every intervention attempt within the grace period should be documented. If the grace period expires without payment, the lapse is recorded but the policyholder should continue to receive communication for a defined period about revival options.

blocks.h: A conservation programme is a structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who are considering or have initiated a surrender or cancellation. Unlike lapse management (which focuses on missed premiums), conservation programmes address the policyholder who has actively decided they want out.

Conservation interventions require a different skill set from standard agent interaction: the conservation specialist must understand the policyholder’s concerns, address misconceptions about the policy’s value, present alternatives to surrender, and — where surrender is genuinely in the policyholder’s interest — process it efficiently and with goodwill. Conservation is not about persuading policyholders to stay against their financial interest; it is about ensuring they have all the information they need to make a genuinely informed decision.

Common alternatives presented in conservation conversations: premium reduction through sum assured adjustment; conversion to paid-up status; policy loan to fund a short-term cash need without surrendering; alteration to a more affordable premium payment frequency; and, where available, reduction riders or product switching.

A policy revival campaign targets lapsed policyholders — those whose policies have already passed the grace period and are technically in lapsed status — with an invitation to reinstate their coverage. Revival is commercially attractive: the original policyholder has already been underwritten and has demonstrated willingness to pay for insurance; the cost of reactivating them is significantly lower than acquiring a new customer.

A well-designed revival campaign includes: a targeted segment of lapsed policyholders (typically those who lapsed within the past 12–24 months, before the coverage gap becomes a major underwriting concern); a compelling reactivation offer (reduced reinstatement medical requirements for policyholders who lapsed recently; waiver of interest on missed premiums for policyholders who reinstate within a defined window; a revised lower premium on reinstatement); and personalised outreach through the original agent plus direct insurer communication (SMS, WhatsApp, email).

From a NAICOM regulatory perspective, reinstated policies may be subject to a new suicide clause period from the reinstatement date. This must be clearly disclosed to the reinstating policyholder as part of the revival documentation.

An existing policyholder is the easiest customer to sell to: the trust barrier has been overcome, the KYC process has been completed, and the customer’s financial profile is partially known. Cross-selling (selling a different product to an existing customer) and upselling (increasing the coverage or value of the existing product) generate premium income at a fraction of the Customer Acquisition Cost of new customer acquisition.

blocks.h: Cross-selling to existing customers is subject to the same suitability obligations as any new insurance sale. An insurer that uses the data it holds about an existing policyholder to target them with an unsuitable product — for example, marketing an investment-linked product to a policyholder whose financial profile suggests they have no risk tolerance or investable surplus — is engaging in potential mis-selling.

The insurer’s cross-sell protocols must include: a suitability assessment before any cross-sell approach (using the policyholder’s known financial profile to identify appropriate products); clear separation between service interactions (a premium collection call should not become a cross-sell pitch without the policyholder’s knowledge); and compliance review of any cross-sell scripts or materials used by contact centre agents or field agents. NIIRA 2025’s treating customers fairly obligation applies to cross-selling as fully as it applies to new customer acquisition.

A referral programme is a structured incentive that rewards existing policyholders for introducing new customers to the insurer. Referrals from satisfied policyholders are the highest-quality leads in insurance: they arrive with a level of social proof and predisposition to purchase that cold leads lack; they convert at higher rates; and they tend to have higher average premium values because the referrer has pre-qualified the prospect.

A well-designed referral programme: offers a reward that is genuinely valuable to the referrer (a premium discount, a gift, or a donation to a named charity in the referrer’s name rather than a cash payment, which can create regulatory complications); makes the referral process frictionless (a simple WhatsApp share, an app referral link, or a verbal introduction at the next policy review); tracks referral outcomes systematically so the referring policyholder can see when their referral has converted; and complies with the NDPA 2023 requirements on data use (the referred prospect must consent to contact before they are reached by the insurer).

An affinity group is a defined population of people who share a common characteristic, institutional relationship, or membership — alumni of a university, members of a professional body, employees of a single employer, members of a trade association — to whom the insurer offers tailored insurance products at group rates or with simplified underwriting.

Affinity marketing is one of the most efficient acquisition models in insurance: the insurer reaches a defined, pre-qualified population through a trusted intermediary (the alumni association, the professional body’s membership communications, the employer’s HR portal); the group discount or simplified access creates a compelling offer; and the institutional endorsement reduces the trust barrier. Nigerian professional associations — ICAN (accountants), NMA (medical doctors), NBA (lawyers), CIIN (insurance professionals) — are natural affinity group partners for life insurance with occupational income protection and group life products.

An employer portal is a digital platform through which an employer’s workforce can access, enrol in, and manage the insurance benefits available to them. It sits at the intersection of worksite marketing (the distribution approach described in Chapter 17) and digital self-service: it gives employees 24/7 access to their benefit elections, coverage details, and enrolment options without requiring a dedicated HR or benefits administration team to process each transaction manually.

A well-designed employer portal enables: online enrolment for new employees; digital beneficiary nomination; coverage summary and policy certificate download; premium contribution statement (for payroll deduction schemes); and integration with the employer’s payroll system for seamless deduction management. The portal reduces the employer’s administrative burden and increases employee engagement with their benefits — employees who actively manage their benefits are more likely to value them and less likely to lapse their individual add-on covers.

A digital acquisition funnel is the end-to-end digital pathway through which a prospective customer moves from first awareness of the insurer’s brand to a completed policy application. Digital funnels convert the investment made in marketing (Chapter 19) into measurable policy issuances by managing the prospect’s journey through defined stages: awareness (reached via social media, search, or display advertising); interest (captured via a lead magnet, premium calculator, or educational content); consideration (nurtured via email sequences or WhatsApp conversations); and decision (converted via a simplified online application or agent handoff).

The critical success factors for Nigerian insurance digital funnels: speed of response after lead capture (same-day contact); simplicity of the application process (mobile-optimised, minimal fields); transparent benefit illustrations (presented in consumer-friendly format before the application); and a clear, trusted payment mechanism (integration with major mobile money platforms and bank transfer). Funnels that require the prospect to switch from digital to physical to complete the purchase (print and sign the form; attend a branch) suffer high abandonment at the switch point.

blocks.text: 20.9 Vulnerable Customer Management and Inclusive Service Design

blocks.h: A customer who, due to their personal circumstances, is at significantly greater risk of harm from the insurer’s actions or inactions than a typical customer. Vulnerability may be temporary (a bereavement, a sudden illness), cyclical (a mental health condition), or permanent (low literacy, a disability, advanced age with cognitive decline). Vulnerability does not mean the customer is incapable; it means they need adapted service to receive the same standard of outcome as a non-vulnerable customer.
Categories of customer vulnerability relevant to Nigerian life insurance:

items.h: Bereavement: A policyholder’s family member presenting a death claim is, almost by definition, in a state of acute emotional vulnerability. Every claims interaction with a bereaved family must be handled with this awareness.

Low financial literacy: A policyholder who does not understand the key terms of their policy — how surrenders work, what the exclusions are, what their beneficiary options are — is at risk of making harmful financial decisions based on incomplete understanding.
Low digital literacy: Policyholders who are unable to use digital self-service platforms are excluded from channels that the insurer may be progressively deprioritising relative to physical channels.

Elderly customers: Older policyholders may have reduced cognitive capacity for complex financial decisions, be particularly susceptible to pressure-selling tactics, and may have physical limitations that affect their ability to visit branches or use digital interfaces.

Financial distress: A policyholder in acute financial hardship who is considering surrendering a long-term policy for its surrender value may not be aware of the paid-up option or other alternatives. An insurer that processes a surrender without proactively presenting alternatives to a financially distressed customer is failing its duty of care.

blocks.h: Vulnerable customers are not always identifiable from their policy records. They may reveal their vulnerability in the course of a customer service interaction: a claimant who mentions that the deceased was the sole breadwinner; a policyholder who struggles to understand an agent’s explanation and repeatedly asks for clarification; a caller who is clearly in distress.

Contact centre agents and field agents must be trained to: recognise the indicators of vulnerability; record the vulnerability on the customer’s file (with appropriate data protection safeguards); adapt their communication style (simpler language, more time, no sales pressure); and escalate to a specialist vulnerability team or supervisor for cases requiring more intensive support.

Adapted service protocols for vulnerable customers: additional time on calls without pressure; written confirmation of all verbal commitments; referral to the insurer’s financial hardship programme where available; third-party advocacy (allowing a family member or community adviser to assist the customer with their interaction); and access to alternative formats for policy documents (larger print, simplified summary in local language).

Inclusive service design is the practice of designing products, processes, and interfaces so that they are accessible and usable by the widest possible range of customers, including those with disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access. In the Nigerian insurance context, inclusive design addresses: USSD-first interfaces for feature phone users; Yoruba, Hausa, and Igbo language options for non-English-comfortable users; visual and audio-format policy summaries for low-literacy users; and branch accessibility for mobility-impaired customers.

Inclusive design is both an ethical obligation and a commercial opportunity. The populations that standard insurance design serves poorly — rural, low-literacy, elderly, informal economy participants — are also the populations where insurance penetration is lowest. Designing for inclusivity expands the addressable market while fulfilling the insurer’s duty of care under NIIRA 2025.

blocks.text: 20.10 NIIRA 2025: NAICOM Consumer Protection Framework and Complaints Redress

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 consolidates and strengthens the consumer protection obligations that were previously scattered across the Insurance Act 2003, NAICOM market conduct guidelines, and CBN consumer protection frameworks. The NIIRA 2025 consumer protection framework is built around six principles that every licensed insurer must observe in all its dealings with policyholders and prospective customers:

rows: Insurers must treat all customers fairly at all stages of the customer relationship — marketing, product design, sales, servicing, and claims. Unfair treatment includes: applying different standards to customers based on protected characteristics; using terms that are unreasonably difficult to understand; and applying policy conditions in a manner inconsistent with the customer’s reasonable expectations.

All material information about a product — premium, coverage, exclusions, surrender value basis, commission paid to intermediaries — must be disclosed to the customer before the policy is concluded, in plain language, and in a format the customer can reasonably be expected to understand.

Products must be sold to customers for whom they are suitable. A complex investment-linked product must not be sold to a customer with no financial sophistication or surplus investable income. The suitability assessment must be documented.

Every insurer must have a written complaints handling policy, a dedicated complaints function, a clear complaints procedure communicated to all customers, and a defined timeline for complaint acknowledgement and resolution.

Customer data must be collected and processed in accordance with the NDPA 2023. Customers must be informed of how their data is used and must be able to exercise their data rights (access, correction, erasure) without unnecessary obstacle.

Insurers must identify and make appropriate accommodations for vulnerable customers, ensuring they receive an equivalent standard of outcome as non-vulnerable customers despite their individual circumstances.

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 establishes a formal multi-tier complaints redress mechanism for insurance consumers. The mechanism works progressively: the complaint must first be addressed internally by the insurer, and only if the internal resolution process fails or the customer is dissatisfied with the outcome may the complaint be escalated externally.

blocks.title: NIIRA 2025: The Three-Tier Complaints Redress Process

blocks.h: TIER 1 — INTERNAL INSURER RESOLUTION: The policyholder submits their complaint to the insurer’s designated complaints officer. The insurer must acknowledge the complaint within the prescribed timeframe and resolve it within the SLA timeline. The insurer must communicate the outcome in writing with clear reasons. If the policyholder is satisfied, the process ends.

TIER 2 — NAICOM CONSUMER PROTECTION DEPARTMENT: If the policyholder is dissatisfied with the insurer’s internal resolution, or if the insurer fails to respond within the prescribed timeframe, the complaint may be referred to NAICOM’s Consumer Protection Department. NAICOM will review the complaint, request information from the insurer, and issue a finding. NAICOM’s finding may direct the insurer to pay the claim, amend its decision, or provide an explanation. NAICOM’s finding is binding on the insurer.

TIER 3 — LEGAL AND ADR: Policyholders retain the right to pursue the matter through the courts or through Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms, including arbitration and mediation, if they are dissatisfied with the NAICOM resolution process. NIIRA 2025 does not extinguish any policyholder’s right to judicial redress.

blocks.text: 20.10.3 NAICOM Enforcement Powers in Respect of Consumer Protection

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 gives NAICOM substantial enforcement powers in response to consumer protection failures. These powers escalate from administrative remedies to existential regulatory consequences:

items.h: Financial penalties: NAICOM may impose financial penalties on insurers that systematically fail to meet consumer protection obligations — including claims payment failures, non-compliant marketing, and inadequate complaints handling.

Public disclosure: NAICOM may publicly name insurers with persistent consumer protection failures in its regulatory bulletins, market conduct reports, and website. Reputational consequences of public naming are a powerful deterrent.

Business restrictions: NAICOM may suspend an insurer’s authority to write new business in specific product lines or through specific channels pending remediation of identified consumer protection failures.

Management intervention: NAICOM may direct the removal or replacement of the Head of Customer Experience, Customer Service Director, or other responsible officers where NAICOM has determined that management failure is the root cause of the consumer protection problem.

Licence revocation: In cases of systematic, serious, and unresolved consumer protection failure, NAICOM may revoke the insurer’s operating licence. This is the most extreme sanction and is reserved for the most serious cases.

blocks.text: 20.11 Advisory: Building a Customer Experience Function for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: A customer experience function that genuinely transforms the policyholder’s experience requires more than a renamed customer service department. It requires organisational commitment, management accountability, technology investment, and a cultural shift toward customer-centricity that must be led from the top.

blocks.title: Advisory: The Customer Experience Maturity Ladder for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: Most Nigerian life insurers currently sit at Level 1 or 2 of the following CX maturity ladder. The NIIRA 2025 regulatory environment and competitive pressures are driving the need to reach Level 3 and 4:

LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE: Customer service is treated as a complaint-handling function. No proactive communication with policyholders between premium collection and claims. No formal SLAs. No CX metrics tracked. Contact centre staffed primarily for inbound complaint management.

LEVEL 2 — OPERATIONAL: Formal SLAs exist and are tracked. A complaints handling policy is documented. Contact centre handles standard queries. Annual statements are sent. There is no proactive lapse management programme. Customer feedback is collected sporadically.

LEVEL 3 — CUSTOMER-CENTRIC: NPS is measured and tracked. Customer journey maps are documented. A proactive lapse management programme operates. Conservation and revival programmes run regularly. Cross-sell is managed systematically. Vulnerable customer protocols are documented and trained. Digital self-service covers 70%+ of routine transactions.

LEVEL 4 — CX-LED GROWTH: CX metrics are Board-level KPIs. The Head of Customer Experience is an Executive Committee member. NPS is >30. Claims storytelling is a central marketing activity. The referral programme generates 20%+ of new business. Customer effort scores drive operational improvement priorities. The insurer is known in the market for the quality of its claims experience.

blocks.title: The Single Most Impactful CX Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: If an insurer can only make one investment in customer experience, it should be in the claims experience. This is true for every life insurer globally, but it is especially true in Nigeria, where the trust deficit is primarily driven by claims payment failures and the fear of them.

Specifically: invest in a proactive claims communication system that sends an automated update to every claimant every 5 business days while their claim is open. This single process change — which requires only a modest technology implementation and a modest increase in contact centre capacity — will reduce complaint rates, improve NPS, generate more claimant testimonials, and create a claims experience that policyholders actually talk about positively. In a market where the fear of ‘they won’t pay’ is the primary purchase barrier, an insurer that demonstrably communicates throughout the claims process is not just providing good service — it is rewriting the industry narrative.

Every interaction a policyholder has with an insurer across the full relationship lifecycle — from awareness through purchase, in-force servicing, and claims — and the cumulative impression those interactions create.

A structured representation of every significant interaction a customer has with the insurer, documenting the customer’s goals, emotional state, pain points, and the insurer’s moments of truth at each stage.

A specific customer interaction at which the customer forms a definitive impression of the organisation that either builds or destroys their trust. The claim payment is the ultimate moment of truth in insurance.
A commitment by the insurer to deliver a defined standard of service within a defined timeframe. SLAs convert subjective service quality into measurable, manageable performance targets.
A customer loyalty metric calculated as the percentage of Promoters (those scoring 9–10 on a recommendation likelihood question) minus the percentage of Detractors (those scoring 0–6).
A transaction-level metric measuring customer satisfaction with a specific interaction, typically on a 1–5 or 1–10 scale administered immediately after the interaction.

A metric measuring how easy it was for a customer to complete an interaction, rated on a scale from ‘strongly disagree’ to ‘strongly agree’ with the statement ‘the company made it easy to handle my issue.’
The proportion of customer queries resolved in the first interaction, without the customer needing to call back or escalate. A measure of both service quality and operational efficiency.
The systematic process of identifying at-risk policies (those with missed premiums), diagnosing the cause, and intervening before the policy moves from active to lapsed status.

A structured set of interventions designed to retain policyholders who are considering or have initiated a surrender or cancellation, by presenting alternatives and ensuring the customer has full information to make a genuinely informed decision.

The reinstatement of a lapsed policy, typically involving repayment of overdue premiums and satisfying any re-underwriting requirements. Revival campaigns target lapsed policyholders with incentives to reinstate.

The sale of a different insurance product to an existing policyholder, based on their existing relationship with the insurer and the expanded coverage need identified from their known financial profile.
Increasing the coverage amount or adding riders to an existing policy, expanding the policyholder’s protection and the insurer’s premium income from the existing relationship.
A structured incentive that rewards existing policyholders for introducing new customers, leveraging social proof and personal endorsement as acquisition tools.

A defined population sharing a common characteristic or institutional membership to whom insurance is offered at group rates or with simplified underwriting, using the institutional relationship as a distribution and trust pathway.

A customer who, due to personal circumstances (bereavement, illness, low literacy, financial distress, advanced age), is at greater risk of harm from the insurer’s actions or inactions than a typical customer.

The practice of designing products, processes, and interfaces to be accessible and usable by the widest possible range of customers, including those with disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access.

A hybrid service delivery model combining physical presence (agent, branch) with digital enablement (app, USSD, WhatsApp), providing human interaction where needed and digital efficiency for routine transactions.

items.h: Pine II, B.J. and Gilmore, J.H. The Experience Economy (updated edn, Harvard Business Review Press, 2019). The foundational text on experience as a commercial and strategic discipline.

Dixon, M., Freeman, K., and Toman, N. ‘Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers.’ Harvard Business Review, July–August 2010. The original Customer Effort Score research demonstrating that reducing effort drives loyalty more effectively than ‘delight.’
Reichheld, F.F. ‘The One Number You Need to Grow.’ Harvard Business Review, December 2003. The foundational Net Promoter Score paper.
Carlzon, J. Moments of Truth (Harper Business, 1987). The seminal text on service management and moments of truth.
McKinsey & Company. ‘How to Create an Insurance Customer Experience.’ mckinsey.com. Framework for CX transformation in insurance with metrics and investment guidance.
Salesforce Research. ‘State of the Connected Customer: Financial Services Edition.’ salesforce.com.
EY. ‘Global Insurance Consumer Survey.’ ey.com. Annual survey including sub-Saharan Africa data on insurance consumer expectations and satisfaction drivers.
LIMRA International. ‘Life Insurance Lapse Causes and Lapse Prevention.’ limra.com. Primary research on lapse causes and intervention effectiveness.
Swiss Re Institute. ‘Bancassurance Persistency: Lessons from Emerging Markets.’ swissre.com.

Financial Conduct Authority (UK). ‘FCA Guidance for Firms on the Fair Treatment of Vulnerable Customers.’ fca.org.uk. The international benchmark for vulnerable customer treatment that informed NIIRA 2025’s provisions.
International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS). ‘Application Paper on Conduct of Business in Inclusive Insurance.’ iaisweb.org.
Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (NIIRA) 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025). Consumer protection framework; complaints redress mechanism; mandatory SLAs; vulnerable customer provisions. naicom.gov.ng.
NAICOM. Consumer Protection Framework and Market Conduct Guidelines. naicom.gov.ng.
Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA). Customer data rights applicable to CX data collection and marketing. ndpc.gov.ng.
